criterion_notes.c1: Does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access. This is an industrial-organization economics study measuring Harberger deadweight allocative welfare loss from monopoly pricing (divergence between price and long-run marginal cost) among existing residential customer classes of U.S. municipal water utilities for comparison with manufacturing-sector monopoly welfare losses.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, this clearly qualifies (yes) because it tests an institutional/regulatory factor: state public utility commission regulation of municipal water utility rate structures (in five states) versus local regulation by city councils or water commissions. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification, utility regulatory structure and tariff/rate-structure regulation fall within the enumerated rule-type categories rather than generic project delivery or behavioural promotion, though in this paper the regulatory mechanism is analyzed only in relation to allocative price-marginal cost efficiency rather than directly governing household service access. Under both the plain and narrow readings of Criterion 2, the overall decision is exclude because Criteria 1 and 4 are not met.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains quantitative empirical evidence using cross-sectional data from the 1965 and 1960 American Water Works Association Survey of Operating Data (OLS regressions on n=95 and n=87 utilities to estimate long-run marginal cost, and two-group comparisons of n=88 locally regulated and n=27 state-regulated municipal water utilities).
criterion_notes.c4: Fails Criterion 4: the sole outcome reported comparing regulatory regimes (Table 2) is theoretical Harberger deadweight welfare loss as a percentage of the residential customer's annual water bill/revenue. It reports no outcome measuring service access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, water quantity delivered/consumed, household affordability (e.g., expenditure-to-income burden or ability to pay; indeed the author notes water has a low cost while focusing on percentage deadweight allocative loss), or exclusion/disconnection.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (U.S. municipally owned water utilities and their aggregate residential customer classes), exposure (state PUC vs. local rate regulation), outcome (deadweight welfare loss as % of annual residential water revenue), and cross-sectional econometric design are clearly identifiable.

evidence_quotes.quote: Despite the low cost of water, sizeable welfare losses seem to exist in the municipal water industry. These percentages are higher than the 0.5 to 7 per cent range reported in the manufacturing sector, mentioned at the outset, and warrant public policy attention.

The welfare loss estimates are divided into two groups, one for utilities that are regulated by state public utility commissions (five states) and one for utilities that are locally regulated by the city council

raw_response.exposure: State public utility commission regulation of municipal water utility rate structures (five states) versus local regulation by city councils or water commissions
raw_response.outcome: Monopoly deadweight welfare loss (Harberger allocative loss triangle from price-marginal cost divergence) expressed as a percentage of the residential customer class's annual water bill/revenue
raw_response.population_and_sample: Municipally owned water utilities in the United States from the 1965 and 1960 American Water Works Association Survey of Operating Data (95 utilities for variable cost and distribution loss equations, 87 for fixed cost equation; 88 locally regulated and 27 state-regulated utilities for welfare-loss comparison; unit of analysis: water utility)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded (E04: Wrong outcome; also does not examine service access under Criterion 1). Although the paper empirically compares state public utility commission regulation versus local municipal regulation of water utility rate structures using 1960/1965 AWWA utility survey data, it is an industrial-organization study of allocative efficiency whose sole outcome is the Harberger deadweight welfare-loss triangle expressed as a percentage of utility residential revenue. It does not examine household or community water service access and reports no outcome measuring connection, availability, reliability, water quantity, household affordability, or exclusion.
